method: Headlines from the source feed, read by Claude: summary and four beats in Blue Street's own words from each article's headline and public text; impact = which way the headline pushes each market (dir bullish/bearish/mixed, strength 1 mild, 2 clear, 3 strong). Evidence, not a call.

USD.text: The dollar sits near its highest since April 2025 because Federal Reserve officials keep backing more rate rises, and Governor Christopher Waller said on Wednesday, November 18 that a half-point rise in December should be considered. Housing figures the same day were mixed, and the minutes of the Fed's October meeting, out at 2:00 PM New York time that day, will show how widely that push is shared.

EUR.text: The euro hovers around $1.10, near its lowest since April 2025, because the Federal Reserve looks set to keep raising rates. European Central Bank Vice President Boris Vujcic said on Wednesday, November 18 that a December rise is very likely after inflation was confirmed at 4%, which gives the euro some support but not enough to offset the Fed.

GBP.text: The pound fell to its lowest against the dollar in about a month after UK inflation for October, released on Wednesday, November 18, came in at 3.6% with core prices steady, and traders cut the odds of a December Bank of England rise to about 80%. Governor Andrew Bailey said the same day that the jobs market has stopped weakening, which keeps that rise possible but did not change the picture much.

JPY.text: The dollar sits just under 160 yen because US rates are far above Japan's. Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda told parliament on Wednesday, November 18 that rates will keep rising and warned a weak yen lifts food prices, but gave no date, and calmer stock markets after Nvidia's results reduce safe-haven demand for the yen.

CHF.text: The Swiss franc sits near a one-month low against a dollar lifted by bets on more Federal Reserve rate rises. Iran's attacks spreading to Kuwait and US strikes on Iranian soil add some demand for the franc as a safe place, while Nvidia's strong results on Tuesday, November 17 ease the stock-market worries that had also helped it.

CAD.text: Canadian inflation held at 3.1% in October, slightly below forecast, and the Bank of Canada's core measures sit near its 2% goal, so a December rate rise looks less likely. Oil, Canada's main export, ended Tuesday, November 17 a little higher but is still down about a fifth this month, and the US dollar is strong, so the Canadian dollar has little to lean on.

AUD.text: The Australian dollar has been the weakest major currency this past month as US rates rise and big banks call the Reserve Bank of Australia's rate rises finished. Faster pay growth, reported on Wednesday, November 18, and calmer share markets after Nvidia's strong results give it some support.

NZD.text: The New Zealand dollar sits near 55 US cents, held down by the strong US dollar. Nvidia's strong results on Tuesday, November 17 calmed share markets, a small help, and dairy prices were flat at the latest auction.

XAU.text: Gold's London afternoon price was set near $3,768 an ounce on Wednesday, November 18, the lowest since late September 2025, after Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller raised the idea of a half-point rate rise in December. Iran's widening attacks in the Gulf have not drawn enough safe-haven buying to offset higher US rates and a strong dollar.

OIL.text: Oil has lost about a fifth this month as Middle East exports recover, and official figures on Wednesday, November 18 showed US crude and gasoline stocks rising far more than expected, pushing prices down about 2%. Attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz and Iran's strikes on its neighbours keep supply scares alive before the OPEC+ meeting on November 29.

items.headline: US crude stocks, gasoline and distillate inventories rise, EIA says
items.story_title: Oil supply: how much is lost to the war, and how fast it comes back
items.summary: Official US figures showed crude stocks up 3.4 million barrels and gasoline up 5.2 million last week, far more than forecast, and oil fell about 2%.

beats.was: Oil has lost about a fifth this month as Middle East exports recover after the Iran war disrupted them, and an industry survey on Tuesday, November 17 had already pointed to a large rise in US crude stocks.
beats.happened: The US Energy Information Administration said on Wednesday, November 18 that crude stocks rose to about 418 million barrels in the week to November 13, against forecasts of almost no change. Gasoline stocks jumped by more than three times the expected amount, and stocks of diesel and heating oil also rose.
beats.means: More oil and fuel is sitting in US storage than expected, a sign that supply is running ahead of demand. That adds to the pressure from returning Gulf exports.
beats.fx: Brent fell to about $92 a barrel and US crude to about $84, a small weight on oil-linked currencies such as the Canadian dollar.

impact.why: Much larger than expected rises in US crude and fuel stocks point to plenty of supply.
Lower oil prices cut into the value of Canada's main export.

items.watch: Whether attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz cut Gulf exports again, and what OPEC+ decides on November 29.

items.headline: US home building rebounds in October, but new permits fall sharply
items.story_title: US housing under high mortgage rates
items.summary: US housing starts rose to a 1.31 million yearly pace in October, above forecasts, but building permits, which point to future building, dropped more than 7%.

beats.was: US mortgage rates have climbed to about 7.2% since the Iran war began in late February, and homebuilder confidence is at its lowest since 2012.
beats.happened: Figures released on Wednesday, November 18 showed housing starts up almost 10% in October, after a weak September. Permits fell to about 1.30 million, well short of forecasts, with single-family permits down almost 9%.
beats.means: The rise in starts looks like a one-month bounce, while the drop in permits shows builders pulling back. Higher rates are hurting housing, but not enough to change the Fed's plan to keep raising.
beats.fx: Little effect on the dollar, which stayed flat after the release.

impact.why: Starts beat forecasts while permits fell sharply, so the report cuts both ways.

items.watch: Whether October existing-home sales also weaken, and whether Fed officials point to housing as a reason to slow.

items.headline: Fed Governor Waller says a half-point rate rise in December should be on the table
items.story_title: The Fed's rate rises and the strong dollar
items.summary: Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said on Wednesday, November 18 that the Fed may need to raise rates by half a point in December, twice the step markets expect, because price rises are spreading across the economy.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve has been raising rates to fight inflation pushed up by energy costs and tariffs, and markets already saw a quarter-point rise at the December 8-9 meeting as close to certain.
beats.happened: In a CNBC interview, Waller said inflation is heading the wrong way and now reaches most service prices, not just fuel. He argued a bigger half-point step may be needed to jolt expectations, unless the Fed signals another rise in January.
beats.means: Waller sits on the Fed's board and often moves ahead of his colleagues, so this raises the chance of a faster pace even if most officials still prefer quarter-point steps. US yields and the dollar rose, while shares and gold fell.
beats.fx: More pressure on the euro, yen and other currencies against the dollar, and on gold, which pays no interest.

impact.why: A Fed governor floating a bigger rate rise lifted US yields and the dollar.
Higher US rates make gold, which pays no interest, less attractive.
A wider gap between US and Japanese rates weighs on the yen.
The euro loses ground when the Fed looks set to keep raising faster than the ECB.

items.watch: Whether the October meeting minutes and other Fed officials back a half-point step, or stick with quarter-point rises.

items.headline: ECB's Vujcic says a December rate rise is very likely on current conditions
items.story_title: Will the ECB raise rates one last time in December?
items.summary: European Central Bank Vice President Boris Vujcic said on Wednesday, November 18 that, as things stand, a rate rise at the December meeting is very likely, and that higher energy costs will feed into wages and other prices in 2027.

beats.was: The European Central Bank has raised rates twice this year as energy costs from the Iran war pushed euro-area inflation to 4%, and markets already expect one more rise at its meeting on Thursday, December 17.
beats.happened: Vujcic, the bank's second most senior official, said a December rise looks very likely based on current conditions, and that so-called second-round effects, where higher energy costs spread into pay and other prices, will definitely show up in 2027.
beats.means: This backs what markets already expect for December. The warning about 2027 hints that rates may not stop there, though the words 'on current conditions' leave room to change course.
beats.fx: A small lift for the euro, since it supports higher euro-area rates for longer. Bets on more Federal Reserve rises still weigh more on the euro against the dollar.

impact.why: The ECB's vice president backs a December rise and warns price pressure will last into 2027.

items.watch: Euro-area business surveys in late November and whether other ECB officials talk about rises beyond December.

items.headline: Fed minutes from October and weak US housing figures due Wednesday, November 18
items.story_title: The Fed's rate rises and the strong dollar
items.summary: The Federal Reserve publishes the minutes of its October meeting at 2:00 PM New York time on Wednesday, November 18, after October housing starts, forecast near a very low 1.25 million a year.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve has been raising rates to cool inflation and several officials have recently backed more rises, so markets see a December rise as close to certain and the dollar near its highest since April 2025.
beats.happened: The minutes will show how many officials at the October meeting wanted to keep raising rates. Before that, October figures on new home building and permits come out, with forecasts pointing to one of the weakest readings in years, and pending home sales follow.
beats.means: The minutes are partly out of date because hotter inflation data and officials' speeches came after the meeting, but a broad push for more rises would back the current pricing. Weak housing shows higher rates are biting.
beats.fx: A firm tone in the minutes would support the dollar; very weak housing figures would lean against it a little.

impact.why: Minutes may back further rate rises, while housing data is expected to be weak.
Gold has been falling as US rate expectations rise, so the tone of the minutes matters.

items.watch: How many October voters wanted more than one further rate rise, and whether housing starts fall below forecast.

items.headline: Euro-area inflation confirmed at 4% as the ECB warns France over its debts
items.story_title: Will the ECB raise rates one last time in December?
items.summary: Eurostat confirmed on Wednesday, November 18 that euro-area prices rose 4% in the year to October, the highest in three years, backing another European Central Bank rate rise in December; the same day the ECB told heavily indebted countries, naming France, to rein in spending.

beats.was: The European Central Bank has raised rates twice this year as energy costs from the Iran war pushed up prices. The early estimate on Tuesday, November 4 had already put October inflation at 4%, up from 3.8% in September.
beats.happened: Eurostat's final figures kept October inflation at 4%, against 2.1% a year earlier. In its twice-yearly Financial Stability Review, the ECB said indebted governments must control spending or face higher borrowing costs, singled out France ahead of its presidential election next year, and said it is not the ECB's job to prop up any one country.
beats.means: The inflation number adds little new because it matches the early estimate, but it keeps a December rise on track. The warning on France is a reminder that wider gaps between French and German borrowing costs could become a worry for the euro.
beats.fx: Roughly balanced for the euro: higher rates support it, while worries about French debt weigh on it. The Fed's own rate rises still matter more for the euro against the dollar.

impact.why: Confirmed 4% inflation backs a December ECB rise, but the warning on French debt is a drag.

items.watch: The euro-area business surveys due in late November, and French borrowing costs compared with Germany's.

items.headline: France and Germany reportedly agree how to share top ECB jobs; Spain's de Cos in line for president
items.story_title: Will the ECB raise rates one last time in December?
items.summary: France and Germany are reported to have agreed a share-out of top European Central Bank jobs, with Spain's Pablo Hernandez de Cos as president and German economist Markus Brunnermeier as chief economist.

beats.was: ECB President Christine Lagarde is leaving early, and euro-area leaders aim to pick her successor in December. The main rivals were Spain's Pablo Hernandez de Cos, a former Bank of Spain governor, and the Netherlands' Klaas Knot.
beats.happened: Reports on Wednesday, November 18 said Germany would back de Cos if Brunnermeier replaces Philip Lane as chief economist when Lane's term ends in May 2027, and France would take the markets post that Isabel Schnabel leaves on January 4. Leaders meet on November 26 and 27, and the choice needs at least 16 countries holding 65% of the euro area's people.
beats.means: It is a reported deal, not a decision. De Cos is seen as close to the ECB's middle ground, so it suggests little change in direction, while a German chief economist could lean firmer on inflation.
beats.fx: Little direct effect on the euro for now; it mainly removes some uncertainty about who leads the ECB next.

impact.why: An unconfirmed deal that points to steady leadership rather than a change of course.

items.watch: Whether leaders confirm the deal at their November 26 and 27 summit.

items.headline: UK inflation climbs to a one-year high, but traders trim Bank of England rate bets
items.story_title: Bank of England: how far do rates rise?
items.summary: UK prices rose 3.6% in the year to October, as forecast, but below the Bank of England's own 3.7% estimate, and the measures that strip out fuel and food did not rise, so traders cut the odds of a December rate rise.

beats.was: The Bank of England raised rates in November for the first time in three years, citing energy costs linked to the Iran war, and markets had priced about a 90% chance of another rise in December.
beats.happened: The Office for National Statistics said on Wednesday, November 18 that consumer prices rose 3.6% in the year to October, up from 3.5%, driven mainly by fuel and an earlier tobacco tax rise. Core inflation, which leaves out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, held at 2.8%, and prices for services held at 3.7% when a rise was expected.
beats.means: Prices are still rising, but the parts the Bank of England watches most closely for lasting pressure did not speed up. Markets now see about an 80% chance of a December rise, down from about 90%, though they still expect three or four rises by the end of 2027 as household energy bills jump about 20% in January.
beats.fx: A push lower for the pound, which fell to its lowest against the dollar in about a month, because a softer core reading weakens the case for UK rates to keep pace with US rates.

impact.why: Steady core and services prices cut the odds of a December Bank of England rise to about 80% from 90%.

items.watch: UK retail sales for October on Friday, November 20, and any comment from Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey on whether December is still likely.

items.headline: Gold drops below $3,800 to its lowest since September 2025
items.story_title: Gold: rising US rates vs war risk
items.summary: Gold fell about 2% to near $3,778 an ounce on Wednesday, November 18, its lowest in more than a year, as the dollar held near a 19-month high and markets treated a December Federal Reserve rate rise as close to certain.

beats.was: Gold has slid for weeks as Federal Reserve officials lined up behind more rate rises; higher US rates make a metal that pays no interest less attractive and lift the dollar it is priced in.
beats.happened: Spot gold fell 1.9% to about $3,778 in Asian trading on Wednesday, November 18, below $3,800 for the first time since September 2025. Futures pricing showed about a 97% chance of a quarter-point Fed rise in December. Silver, platinum and palladium fell too.
beats.means: Analysts said investors are selling gold to raise cash and because the chart picture has turned weak, not only because of the Fed. Repeated Iranian attacks in the Gulf are not bringing in enough safe-haven buying to offset that.
beats.fx: Clear pressure on gold, and a small extra lift for the dollar story. Minutes from the Fed's October 27-28 meeting, due Wednesday, November 18 at 1:00 PM CT, are the next thing that could shift it.

impact.why: Near-certain Fed rise and a firm dollar pushed gold to a more-than-one-year low.
The same rate bets that sink gold keep the dollar near a 19-month high.

items.watch: The Fed minutes on Wednesday, November 18, November 18; signs officials want fewer rises than markets expect would ease the pressure on gold.

items.headline: Bank of Japan's Ueda repeats that rates will keep rising, warns a weak yen lifts food prices
items.story_title: Will the Bank of Japan raise rates in December?
items.summary: Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda told parliament on Wednesday, November 18 that the bank will keep raising rates because borrowing conditions are still easy, but gave no timing, and warned that a weak yen pushes up food prices.

beats.was: The Bank of Japan held its rate at 1.25% on October 30. The dollar sits just under 160 yen because US rates are far higher than Japan's, and Japan's economy shrank slightly in July to September.
beats.happened: Speaking to an upper-house committee, Ueda said the bank will keep lifting rates in line with the economy, prices and financial conditions. He gave no date for the next rise. He said a weaker yen raises import costs for food, eating into the benefit of the planned cut to the tax on food, and that long-term bond yields should be set by the market rather than held down by emergency bond buying.
beats.means: The message matches what Ueda has said before, so it does little to settle whether the next rise comes in December or later. Naming the weak yen as a cost for households hints the bank is uneasy about it.
beats.fx: A small support for the yen, because it keeps a December rise possible. Without a date, it does not close much of the gap with US rates.

impact.why: Ueda keeps further rate rises on the table and flags the cost of a weak yen, but gives no timing.

items.watch: Japan's October consumer prices on Friday, November 20, and any warning from Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama if the dollar moves above 160 yen.

items.headline: Australian wages post their biggest quarterly rise since 2023
items.story_title: Has the Reserve Bank of Australia finished raising rates?
items.summary: Australian pay rose 1.1% in July to September, above the 0.9% forecast and the fastest quarterly gain since late 2023, which keeps alive the case for another Reserve Bank of Australia rate rise.

beats.was: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates in November on a 6-3 vote, and its minutes showed the board split on whether a fifth rise is needed. Big Australian banks think rates have peaked, and the Australian dollar has been the weakest major currency this past month.
beats.happened: The Australian Bureau of Statistics' Wage Price Index, released on Wednesday, November 18, rose 1.1% in the September quarter against 0.9% expected, taking yearly pay growth to 3.5% from 3.4%. The yearly minimum and award wage rise of 4.75% lifted private pay, and new state deals for nurses, midwives and police lifted public pay.
beats.means: Much of the jump comes from once-a-year pay decisions rather than a tighter jobs market, so it may not last. Still, faster pay growth makes it harder for the central bank to say inflation is beaten, which weakens the banks' call that rates have peaked.
beats.fx: A small lift for the Australian dollar, since it supports the side of the Reserve Bank of Australia board that wants one more rise. It does little against the strong US dollar and falling share markets.

impact.why: Pay grew faster than forecast, backing the case for another Reserve Bank of Australia rise.

items.watch: Australia's October jobs figures on Thursday, November 19, which will show whether the jobs market is still tight.

items.headline: Oil slips as US crude stocks rise
items.story_title: Oil supply: how much is lost to the war, and how fast it comes back
items.summary: Oil edged lower early on Wednesday, November 18, with Brent just under $93 a barrel, after an industry count showed US crude stocks rose by about 5.3 million barrels last week.

beats.was: Oil has lost about a fifth this month as Middle East exports recover and the International Energy Agency forecasts more supply than demand this quarter, but attacks around the Strait of Hormuz keep lifting prices on some days.
beats.happened: The American Petroleum Institute, an industry group, reported on Tuesday, November 17 that US crude stocks grew by about 5.3 million barrels and petrol stocks by about 5.1 million in the week to November 13. Brent fell about 0.2% and US crude about 0.7% in Asian trading. Fresh Gulf attacks, including on a gas tanker near Hormuz, kept the losses small.
beats.means: Rising US stockpiles add to the picture of a well-supplied market, which pulls against the war risk. Analysts at LSEG said shipping through Hormuz is still far from normal, so supply scares can return quickly.
beats.fx: A mild drag on the Canadian dollar, as oil is Canada's main export. Cheaper oil is a slight help for big energy importers such as Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: A large rise in US crude stocks points to ample supply.
Softer oil weighs on Canada's main export.

items.watch: The US government's weekly oil stock figures on Wednesday, November 18, which either confirm or contradict the industry count.

items.headline: Gold and Silver 'Can't Find a Floor' as Waller Calls for Fed Rate Hike
items.story_title: Gold: rising US rates vs war risk
items.summary: Gold's London afternoon price was set near $3,768 on Wednesday, November 18, about $90 lower than a day earlier and the lowest since late September 2025, and silver neared $45.

beats.was: Gold pays no interest, so it tends to lose appeal when US rates rise, and Federal Reserve officials have been backing further rate rises after a hot October inflation report.
beats.happened: Fed Governor Christopher Waller said on Wednesday, November 18 that a half-point rise in December should be considered. Gold then fell as much as 3.6% from its close on Friday, November 13, silver was down as much as 7.5% for the week, and platinum and palladium also dropped.
beats.means: Markets now expect the Fed to raise rates in December and probably again early next year, which makes holding metals costlier against a dollar that earns more.
beats.fx: A stronger dollar and higher US rates keep weighing on gold and silver.

impact.why: A further leg down on bets for bigger and more Fed rate rises.
The same rate-rise bets that hit gold lift the dollar.

items.watch: The minutes of the Fed's October meeting, due at 2:00 PM New York time on Wednesday, November 18, and whether other officials back a half-point rise.

items.headline: US jets hit an Iranian missile site on Qeshm Island; UAE oil company ship attacked in Hormuz
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: US jets struck an Iranian Revolutionary Guards missile site on Qeshm Island on Tuesday, November 17 after drones were fired at a US radar in Bahrain, and a ship run by the UAE's state oil company ADNOC was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz.

beats.was: Iran and the US have traded fire around the Gulf for months; the Strait of Hormuz carries about a fifth of the world's oil, so attacks on shipping there move oil prices.
beats.happened: A US official called the strike on Qeshm Island, which sits inside the Strait of Hormuz, self-defence after Revolutionary Guards drones targeted a US radar at Bahrain's Isa Air Base. An ADNOC Logistics vessel was attacked in the strait, with one crew member missing and 11 hurt, and 24 people were taken off a burning tanker off Oman's Musandam peninsula. Gulf airlines extended flight cancellations to Saudi Arabia.
beats.means: Direct US strikes on Iranian soil and fresh hits on ships make it harder to argue the conflict is cooling, and raise shipping insurance costs through the strait.
beats.fx: Some upward pressure on oil and a mild lift for safe places like the Swiss franc and gold, held back by the bigger story of rising US rates and recovering Gulf oil exports.

impact.why: Ships hit in Hormuz and US strikes on Iran raise the risk to the main Gulf oil route.
Escalation between the US and Iran adds safe-haven demand.
Supply scares support oil, Canada's main export.

items.watch: Whether Iran answers the Qeshm strike, and whether tanker traffic through Hormuz slows.

items.headline: Japan's exports hit a record in October on chip demand
items.story_title: Will the Bank of Japan raise rates in December?
items.summary: Japan's exports rose 20.5% from a year earlier in October to a monthly record, led by chips and chipmaking machines, and the trade gap came in about half as wide as forecast.

beats.was: Japan's economy shrank slightly in July to September, which gave the Bank of Japan a reason to hesitate over the rate rise to 1.5% that markets expect in December. The dollar trades just under 160 yen.
beats.happened: The Ministry of Finance's October trade figures, released on Wednesday, November 18, showed exports up 20.5% on a year earlier, a little above forecasts and the 14th rise in a row. Chip exports jumped by about half, and sales to the US rose about 24%. Imports rose less than expected, so the trade deficit was about 477 billion yen against roughly 956 billion forecast.
beats.means: Demand for AI chips is holding up Japan's factories while Chinese demand stays soft. Part of the jump comes from higher prices rather than more goods shipped, but it still eases worries that the economy is stalling, which helps the case for a December rate rise.
beats.fx: A small help for the yen: stronger trade supports a Bank of Japan rise and a smaller deficit means fewer yen sold to pay for imports. It does little against the wide gap between US and Japanese rates.

impact.why: Record exports and a smaller trade gap support a December Bank of Japan rise.

items.watch: Japan's October inflation figures on Friday, November 20, the last big reading before the Bank of Japan's December meeting.

items.headline: ECB to discuss doubling the cash banks must park with it, sources say
items.story_title: Will the ECB raise rates one last time in December?
items.summary: European Central Bank policymakers will discuss on Wednesday, November 25 doubling the share of deposits that banks must hold at the central bank without earning interest, from 1% to 2%, four sources told Reuters.

beats.was: Euro-area banks hold over €2 trillion of spare cash at the European Central Bank, and as rates have risen the ECB and national central banks now pay out about €52 billion a year in interest on it.
beats.happened: Sources said the Governing Council will weigh raising the minimum reserve, the slice of deposits banks must keep at the central bank unpaid, to 2% at its meeting on Wednesday, November 25, with a decision possibly pushed to Thursday, December 17. Reuters estimates it would save the central banks about €4.4 billion a year. Vice President Boris Vujcic and chief economist Philip Lane are said to support it.
beats.means: It is a technical step to cut the cost of higher rates to the central banks, not a rate change. It would trim bank profits a little and take a small amount of spare cash out of the system.
beats.fx: Little direct effect on the euro. Weaker bank earnings are a small minus, a slightly tighter supply of spare cash a small plus. The ECB has not confirmed it.

impact.why: An unconfirmed technical change that would slightly squeeze banks and slightly tighten cash.

items.watch: Any announcement after the ECB's non-rate meeting on Wednesday, November 25, or at the December 17 policy meeting.

items.headline: BoE's Bailey says the UK jobs market has stopped loosening
items.story_title: Bank of England: how far do rates rise?
items.summary: Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey said on Wednesday, November 18 that the UK jobs market is no longer getting weaker, though some slack remains, and that the next rate decision is not decided in advance.

beats.was: The Bank of England raised rates in November for the first time in three years. UK inflation for October, out on Wednesday, November 18, came in at 3.6% with core prices steady, and traders cut the odds of a December rise to about 80%.
beats.happened: Speaking at a conference in London, Bailey said spare capacity in the jobs market has stopped growing because the economy has picked up, but some remains. He repeated that policy is not on a set path and the bank will judge the evidence that builds up before its next meeting.
beats.means: A jobs market that has stopped loosening makes it harder for pay growth to keep cooling, which leans toward another rise. But Bailey gave no clear steer on December.
beats.fx: A slight support for the pound after the softer core inflation figures, as it keeps a December rise on the table.

impact.why: Bailey says job-market slack has stopped growing, which keeps a December rise alive.

items.watch: UK retail sales for October on Friday, November 20, and the Bank of England's decision on Thursday, December 17.

items.headline: Kuwait and Bahrain fend off Iranian drone attacks as Saudi-led coalition hits Houthi sites
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Iran says its drones targeted US air defences at a base in Kuwait early on Wednesday, November 18, its first attack on Kuwait since September, while Bahrain intercepted more Iranian attacks and the Saudi-led coalition struck about 60 Houthi targets in Yemen.

beats.was: The US-Israel war with Iran has settled into a pattern of drone strikes around the Gulf and attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow route for about a fifth of the world's oil. Iran had resumed drone attacks on Bahrain on Tuesday, November 17 after a two-month lull.
beats.happened: Iran's army said on state television that its drones went after Patriot air defence systems at Ali Al-Salem Air Base in Kuwait, which hosts US forces. Kuwait said the blasts heard were its own interceptions and called the attack a breach of its sovereignty. Bahrain said it stopped several more Iranian attacks. The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said it hit about 60 Houthi sites, including missile tunnels and drone workshops, after intercepting a Houthi cruise missile aimed at Riyadh.
beats.means: The fighting now reaches more Gulf states at once, which raises the risk to oil sites and shipping. So far no oil facility has been reported hit, and oil prices kept falling on rising US stocks.
beats.fx: A mild upward push on oil and on safe places like the Swiss franc. Markets have mostly shrugged off these attacks unless they damage supply.

impact.why: Attacks spreading to Kuwait raise the risk to Gulf oil, though no supply was hit.
Wider Gulf fighting adds some demand for a safe currency.

items.watch: Any hit to an oil terminal, pipeline or tanker route, or a direct US response to the Kuwait attack.

items.headline: Nvidia beats forecasts in its first results since Jensen Huang's exit
items.story_title: The AI stock sell-off before Nvidia's results
items.summary: Nvidia, the chipmaker at the centre of the AI boom, reported sales of $115.8 billion for its latest quarter on Tuesday, November 17, well above the $109 billion expected, and forecast more; its shares rose about 2% after hours.

beats.was: AI-linked shares had fallen hard for days after Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's chief executive on November 12, and the Dow dropped more than 700 points on Monday, November 16. Falling share markets tend to hurt riskier currencies like the Australian and New Zealand dollars and help the yen.
beats.happened: Nvidia's sales doubled from a year earlier, with data-centre chips making up about 93% of them. It expects about $130 billion next quarter, above the roughly $125 billion forecast, even with no data-centre sales to China. Interim chief executive Colette Kress led the call; the board said it is not considering bringing Huang back, and US regulators have opened an investigation.
beats.means: The results show AI spending is still strong, which eases fears that the boom is cracking. The leadership questions remain, so the relief may be limited; the shares are still about a third below their October peak.
beats.fx: A mild lift for share markets and for currencies that rise with them, like the Australian and New Zealand dollars, and a mild drag on the yen and Swiss franc as safe-haven demand eases.

impact.why: Strong AI results calm share markets, which tends to help the Australian dollar.
Calmer share markets support the New Zealand dollar.
Less fear in markets reduces demand for the yen as a safe place.

items.watch: Whether the after-hours gain holds through US trading on Wednesday, November 18, and any news on Nvidia's leadership or the regulator's probe.

items.headline: Houthis claim drone strikes on Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Yemen's Houthi rebels said on Tuesday, November 17 they sent five drones at two pumping stations on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, the route that lets Saudi oil avoid the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed any damage.

beats.was: With shipping through the Strait of Hormuz disrupted by the war with Iran, Saudi Arabia leans on its East-West pipeline, which can carry about 4 million barrels a day to the Red Sea port of Yanbu. The pipeline was shut for a while in September after a drone attack, and the Iran-allied Houthis have claimed several strikes on it this month.
beats.happened: Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said three drones targeted Pumping Station 9 west of Riyadh and two hit Station 8, and claimed large fires. There was no independent confirmation of damage or of any halt to oil flows.
beats.means: The claim alone does not remove any oil, but it shows the main route around Hormuz is a target. If an attack did force a shutdown, a large share of Saudi exports would be stuck.
beats.fx: Little direct effect while the claim is unconfirmed. A confirmed shutdown would lift oil, helping the Canadian dollar and hurting energy importers such as the yen and euro.

impact.why: Unconfirmed claim of drone hits on Saudi Arabia's route around Hormuz.

items.watch: Whether Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry confirms damage or any pause in pipeline flows.

items.headline: Oil ends higher after a $3 swing as Gulf attacks continue
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Brent crude ended Tuesday, November 17 up 0.8% at $93.14 a barrel after swinging about $3 during the day, as attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz weighed against forecasts of too much oil next year.

beats.was: Oil is up more than half this year because of the war with Iran, but it fell earlier in November as Middle East exports through the Strait of Hormuz recovered and the International Energy Agency forecast a supply surplus of about 2 million barrels a day this quarter.
beats.happened: Ships were reported attacked in and around the Strait, Iran targeted Bahrain for the third time in under a week, and a US official said US warplanes hit an Iranian missile site on Qeshm Island. Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran wants a diplomatic way out, and Qatar said it is still trying to mediate.
beats.means: Oil is caught between two forces: plenty of supply on paper and a war that keeps threatening it. Prices tend to rise before weekends on fears of escalation and fall back when nothing happens.
beats.fx: A steady oil price gives the Canadian dollar and Norway's krone a little help after a weak month. For the yen and euro, whose economies import most of their energy, higher oil is a slight drag.

impact.why: Fresh attacks near Hormuz lift Brent despite surplus forecasts.
Oil, Canada's main export, firms up.

items.watch: Weekly US crude stock figures, and any sign that Qatar's mediation brings Iran and the US closer.

items.headline: Fed's Williams sees one more rate rise, nothing dramatic
items.story_title: The Fed's rate rises and the strong dollar
items.summary: New York Fed President John Williams said on Tuesday, November 17 that the Fed will probably need one more rate rise, but he sees no need for big moves. That is calmer than St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem, who spoke of several rises the same day.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve held its main rate at 3.75% to 4.00% in October, but rising prices from tariffs and the Middle East energy shock have pushed several officials to call for more rate rises, lifting the dollar to its highest since April 2025.
beats.happened: Williams, who as head of the New York Fed votes at every meeting and is seen as close to the Fed's centre, said inflation is too high and is spreading beyond the areas first hit by supply problems. He still said one more rise is likely enough for now, and that recent tightening is working.
beats.means: Fed officials agree rates go up again in December but differ on how far after that. A rise of a quarter point on December 9 is almost fully expected, while a half-point move has been all but ruled out.
beats.fx: The dollar keeps its support from a December rise, but Williams makes a long run of rises look less certain, which limits how much further that support stretches.

impact.why: Backs a December rise but pushes back on a long string of them.

items.watch: Minutes of the Fed's October meeting, due Wednesday, November 18, for how many officials want more than one more rise.

items.headline: US dollar pulls back as traders take profits
items.story_title: The Fed's rate rises and the strong dollar
items.summary: The dollar slipped back from its 19-month high on the afternoon of Tuesday, November 17, as traders took some profit and US bond yields eased. The euro rose back above $1.10.

beats.was: The dollar had risen seven days in a row on bets that the Federal Reserve will keep raising rates. That pushed the euro below $1.10 for the first time since April 2025 and the dollar to just under 160 yen.
beats.happened: By late afternoon in London the euro was back near $1.101 and the pound above $1.32, while the dollar fell back from 160 yen as the US two-year Treasury yield dipped below 4.79%. The ZEW survey of financial experts also showed euro-area economic sentiment improving to 26.5, well above the 19.1 forecast.
beats.means: This is a pause after a long run, not a change in the story. The US figures released the same day did nothing to weaken the case for more Fed rate rises.
beats.fx: The euro, pound and yen get a little breathing room. The dollar's main support, higher US interest rates, is still in place.

impact.why: Profit-taking and slightly lower US yields pull the dollar off a 19-month high.
Back above $1.10, helped by a better-than-expected survey of euro-area sentiment.
The dollar eases back from just under 160 yen as US yields dip.

items.watch: Minutes of the Fed's last meeting, due Wednesday, November 18.

items.headline: UK inflation expected to rise to 3.6% in October
items.story_title: Bank of England: how far do rates rise?
items.summary: UK inflation for October, due at 7:00 AM London time on Wednesday, November 18, is expected to climb to 3.6% from 3.5%, pushed up by fuel, household energy and a rise in tobacco duty.

beats.was: UK inflation fell to 2.6% in June, then rose for three months in a row as the Middle East energy shock lifted fuel prices. The Bank of England raised its rate to 4.00% on November 5 and expects inflation to peak around 5% next year.
beats.happened: Forecasters polled by Pantheon Macroeconomics expect 3.6%, which would be a fourth rise in a row and the highest since October 2025. The energy price cap set by the regulator Ofgem went up 4% in October, and higher tobacco and vape duty adds to the monthly jump.
beats.means: A reading at or above forecast backs a further Bank of England rate rise in December. A reading below would ease that pressure, especially after a jobs report on Tuesday, November 17 that showed pay growth cooling.
beats.fx: This is a preview, so it moves little on its own. The pound has slid against a strong dollar, and a high reading would give it some support through higher expected UK rates.

impact.why: Preview only; a high reading would firm up a December Bank of England rise.

items.watch: The October inflation figures on Wednesday, November 18, especially services prices, which the Bank of England watches closely.

items.headline: Global Dairy Prices Stall as New Zealand's GDT Index Flatlines at 0.0%
items.story_title: Dairy prices and New Zealand's export income
items.summary: Global dairy prices were unchanged at the Global Dairy Trade auction on Tuesday, November 17, after a 3% rise at the previous one. Milk powder rose while butter and cheese fell.

beats.was: Dairy is New Zealand's biggest export, so prices at the twice-monthly Global Dairy Trade auction feed into the country's income and the value of its currency. The previous auction had lifted prices by 3%.
beats.happened: The overall price index was flat. Whole milk powder, New Zealand's main dairy product, rose about 2.7% and skim milk powder about 2.2%, while butter fell about 6.5% and cheddar cheese about 4%.
beats.means: The rise in milk powder still helps New Zealand's farmers, but the rally across dairy prices has paused.
beats.fx: A small support for the New Zealand dollar through milk powder, not enough to offset a strong US dollar and falling stock markets.

impact.why: Milk powder prices rose but the overall dairy index was flat after a 3% gain last time.

items.watch: The next Global Dairy Trade auction on Tuesday, December 1, and whether milk powder keeps rising.

items.headline: Wall St falls before Nvidia earnings in key AI test; Huang says open to return
items.story_title: The AI stock sell-off before Nvidia's results
items.summary: US stocks fell for a second day on Tuesday, November 17, with the Dow down about 1.6% by midday, as investors pulled back before chipmaker Nvidia's results after the close. Every sector of the S&P 500 was lower.

beats.was: Technology shares have been sliding for days. Nvidia, the biggest maker of AI chips, has lost about $410 billion in market value since its chief executive Jensen Huang resigned the week before, and AI company Anthropic plans a record stock market listing on Thursday, November 19.
beats.happened: By midday in New York the Dow had dropped about 820 points, the S&P 500 1.3% and the Nasdaq 1.4%, leaving the two broader indexes near their lowest in months. Huang said he would be willing to come back if the board wanted him, though the board was reported not to be considering it. Futures markets put the chance of a Federal Reserve rate rise in December at about 95%.
beats.means: Investors are heading into Nvidia's results already nervous, with rising US interest rates adding to the pressure on share prices.
beats.fx: Falling stock markets tend to weigh on currencies tied to global growth, such as the Australian and New Zealand dollars, and help safe currencies like the yen.

impact.why: A broad US stock sell-off weighs on a currency that tracks global risk appetite.
Falling shares tend to pull the kiwi lower along with the Australian dollar.
Nervous markets tend to send money toward the yen as a safe place.

items.watch: Nvidia's results after the US close on Tuesday, November 17: a strong report could steady stocks, a weak one could deepen the slide.

items.headline: US dollar holds near 19-month high as retail sales support Fed rate hike expectations
items.story_title: The Fed's rate rises and the strong dollar
items.summary: US shoppers kept spending in October: retail sales rose 0.2% and the core measure rose a firmer 0.6%, which backs the case for a Federal Reserve rate rise in December.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve is raising rates to cool inflation, which sped up in October, and markets treat a quarter-point rise at the December 9 meeting as close to certain. Retail sales were the first big test of whether US consumers can handle higher borrowing costs.
beats.happened: Retail sales for October rose 0.2% from September, as expected, after a strong 0.8% gain the month before. The core measure, which leaves out cars, fuel, building materials and restaurants, rose 0.6%, more than forecast, and September's core figure was revised up to 0.5%. The dollar index held near its highest since April 2025.
beats.means: Spending is holding up despite higher rates, so nothing here argues for the Fed to stop. Markets now see almost no chance of a bigger half-point move, but a quarter-point rise stays the clear expectation.
beats.fx: The figures keep the support under the dollar in place rather than adding much to it. They also keep pressure on gold and on currencies like the euro whose central banks are closer to the end of their rate rises.

impact.why: Solid core spending backs a December Fed rate rise.
Firmer US rate expectations keep weighing on gold.
The gap between US and European rate paths stays wide.

items.watch: Minutes of the Fed's October meeting on Wednesday, November 18: signs of a split over more rate rises would test the dollar's climb.

items.headline: St. Louis Fed's Musalem calls for interest rate hikes 'soon'
items.story_title: The Fed's rate rises and the strong dollar
items.summary: Alberto Musalem, head of the St. Louis Federal Reserve, said the Fed should raise rates soon and will likely need several more rises before spring 2027, possibly a full point or more in total.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve's main rate sits at 3.75% to 4% and US inflation is running above 3%, well over the Fed's 2% goal. Markets already see a quarter-point rise at the Fed's December 8-9 meeting as close to certain.
beats.happened: In a speech in Buenos Aires on Tuesday, November 17, Musalem said rates are up to a point below where they need to be. His target implies rises of 1 to 1.5 percentage points by spring, taking the rate to around 4.75% to 5%. He called the economy strong and the job market steady. He does not vote on rates this year.
beats.means: It is one of the clearest calls yet for a long run of rises, not just one in December. Even without a vote, it pushes up the path markets expect for US rates into 2027.
beats.fx: More expected Fed rises support the dollar against the euro, yen and pound, and weigh on gold, which pays no interest.

impact.why: A Fed president sketching a full point or more of rises by spring lifts the expected path of US rates.
Higher expected US rates make gold, which pays no interest, less attractive.
A wider gap between US and Japanese rates keeps pressure on the yen.

items.watch: Minutes of the Fed's last meeting on Wednesday, November 18, for how many officials back more than one more rise.

items.headline: Bahrain intercepts Iranian drones targeting US radar after 2-month lull in Gulf strikes
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Iran fired drones at a US radar in Bahrain on Tuesday, November 17, its third such attack in five days. Bahrain shot them down and the US says nothing was damaged.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war since February, and Iran keeps the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, mostly shut. Bahrain hosts the US Navy's main Gulf base and had seen no Iranian strikes for about two months until Friday, November 13.
beats.happened: On the morning of Tuesday, November 17, Bahrain told residents to take shelter and explosions were heard in the capital, Manama. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they targeted a US radar at the Sheikh Isa air base, calling it a reply to US drones over Iran. US Central Command said the drones were stopped with no damage and no one hurt.
beats.means: Three attacks in five days show Iran is pressing on Gulf states that host US forces, even as Washington signals it may hold off on new strikes. So far none has done real damage.
beats.fx: Each attack adds a little to oil prices and safe-haven demand for the Swiss franc, but markets react less each time as long as nothing is hit.

impact.why: Repeated attacks near Gulf oil routes keep some risk premium in prices.
Gulf tension adds modest demand for the franc as a safe place.

items.watch: Whether an attack causes damage or casualties, and any US military reply.

items.headline: Oman discusses maritime security with Iran amid rising attacks in Strait of Hormuz
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: A tanker was hit twice off Oman overnight and its crew could not be accounted for, while Iran's foreign minister held talks in Oman on keeping sea routes safe.

beats.was: The US and Israel have been at war with Iran since late February, and the Strait of Hormuz, which carried about a fifth of the world's energy before the war, has seen repeated attacks on ships. Oil has still been falling because exports through the strait are recovering.
beats.happened: The UK navy's shipping-alert service said a tanker about 7 nautical miles off Khasab, Oman, was struck on Monday, November 16 night, caught fire in its engine room, and was hit again later; the crew was reported unaccounted for. Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed two more ships hit naval mines in the strait, which has not been confirmed. In Muscat, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi discussed reopening dialogue and protecting shipping.
beats.means: Attacks on shipping keep coming, but traffic and oil prices have mostly shrugged them off. Oman's talks are a small sign that a diplomatic channel stays open.
beats.fx: Each new strike adds a little risk to oil supply, but with prices drifting lower on an expected glut, the push on oil and oil-linked currencies is small.

impact.why: Another tanker hit near Hormuz, though prices have shrugged off similar attacks.
Continued Gulf violence keeps some demand for safe currencies.

items.watch: Whether attacks spread to big crude carriers, and whether the Oman talks lead to any wider contact between Iran and the US.

items.headline: Iran and Oman foreign ministers meet in Muscat with no Hormuz agreement
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met Oman's Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi in Muscat on Tuesday, November 17. The talks ended with no deal or timetable for reopening shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

beats.was: Iran has kept the Strait of Hormuz closed or restricted since July, and the US has a naval blockade on Iran. Oman sits on the strait's southern side and has long passed messages between Tehran and Washington.
beats.happened: The two ministers discussed shipping safety and calming tensions, and Oman called the meeting constructive. Neither side announced an agreement, and the official accounts did not mention Hormuz shipping, which an Omani statement on November 5 had named. Hours earlier another tanker was hit near the strait.
beats.means: The channel for talks stays open, but there is no sign yet that the strait will return to normal traffic soon.
beats.fx: Keeps some war-risk premium in oil, a small help for the Canadian dollar and a cost for big energy importers such as Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: No progress on reopening Hormuz keeps supply worries alive.

items.watch: Any follow-up from Oman or Iran on Hormuz shipping, and the OPEC+ meeting on November 29.

items.headline: UK wage growth slows to 3.5% in three months to September
items.story_title: Bank of England: how far do rates rise?
items.summary: UK pay growth cooled a little more than expected and job openings fell to their lowest since 2021, but unemployment also dipped. The pound barely moved.

beats.was: The Bank of England raised rates in November for the first time in more than three years, because UK inflation is running well above its 2% goal. Markets expect another rise in December, and pay growth is one of the main things the Bank watches.
beats.happened: Regular pay, leaving out bonuses, grew 3.5% from a year earlier in July to September, down from 3.7% and just under forecasts. Unemployment slipped to 4.6% instead of rising, but the tax office's payroll count fell by about 34,000 in October and job openings dropped to 690,000, the fewest since early 2021.
beats.means: Slower pay and fewer openings point to a cooling job market, which takes a little heat out of inflation. It is not weak enough to change the Bank's December plans, so markets still see about a 90% chance of a rise.
beats.fx: A mixed report that leaves the December rate rise in place, so the pound keeps taking its lead from the strong dollar rather than from UK news.

impact.why: Pay and job openings cooled, but unemployment fell; December rise still about 90% expected.

items.watch: UK inflation for October, out Wednesday morning: a high reading would firm up the December rise.

items.headline: RBNZ Survey Shows Near-Term Inflation Fears Rising, but Long-Term Expectations Ease
items.story_title: Will the Reserve Bank of New Zealand raise rates on December 9?
items.summary: Business leaders and forecasters polled by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand now expect inflation of almost 3% over the next year, up from 2.6%. Their longer-run views eased, and they now expect the bank to raise its 2.75% rate soon.

beats.was: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand asks firms and economists every quarter where they see prices and rates heading. Its policy rate is 2.75%, inflation slowed to 3.7% in July to September, and unemployment has risen to 5.7%.
beats.happened: The November survey, out on Tuesday, November 17, showed expected inflation one year ahead rising to 2.92%. The two-year view, which the bank watches most, barely moved at 2.36%, and the five- and ten-year views fell. Respondents now see the policy rate at about 3.05% by the end of this year and 3.40% a year from now, and expect house prices to rise only 0.5%.
beats.means: Price worries are rising in the short run but the longer-run anchor is holding, which gives the bank room to move slowly. Respondents expect a rate rise at the December 9 meeting, but rising joblessness argues for caution.
beats.fx: A small lift for the New Zealand dollar from higher expected rates, but it was offset by the strong US dollar and the kiwi barely moved.

impact.why: Higher expected rates help, but steady long-run expectations and rising unemployment let the bank go slowly.

items.watch: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand's decision on December 9: a rise would match what this survey expects; a hold would hurt the kiwi.

items.headline: Is the US-Israel war on Iran turning into a 'frozen conflict'?
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: President Trump said the US does not need a deal with Iran, while Iran says it will not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until the US lifts its blockade of Iranian ports and its sanctions. Neither side is moving, so the standoff looks set to drag on.

beats.was: The US and Israel went to war with Iran in February 2026. A deal in June fell apart and the US reimposed a naval blockade of Iranian ports in July, and Iran has kept the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for Gulf oil, largely shut.
beats.happened: Trump wrote on his social media site that the US holds both Iranian money and control of the strait and needs no deal. Iran repeated that the strait stays shut until the blockade and sanctions end. Only a handful of cargo ships crossed the strait on some days in early November, and Iran's economy shrank about 10% from a year earlier in the spring.
beats.means: Neither side is under enough pressure to give way, so attacks and disruption at sea look likely to continue without a full war or a settlement.
beats.fx: Keeps a floor under oil prices, since a reopening of Hormuz is not in sight, but recovering exports from elsewhere in the Middle East limit the effect.

impact.why: No reopening of Hormuz in sight supports prices, but recovering Gulf exports cap them.
Canada's oil exports gain from a firm floor under prices, but oil is still well down this month.

items.watch: Any sign of talks between Washington and Tehran, and whether Iran is raised at President Trump's meeting with China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin on Thursday, November 19.

items.headline: Oil prices caught between tanker attacks and rising Mideast exports
items.story_title: Oil supply: how much is lost to the war, and how fast it comes back
items.summary: Oil turned higher on Tuesday, November 17, with Brent near $93.70, after more attacks on Gulf shipping and a US radar in Bahrain, though prices remain far below their October peak.

beats.was: Oil soared when the US-Iran war cut Gulf exports, but Brent has lost about a fifth of its value this month as those exports recover and the International Energy Agency expects more supply than demand this quarter.
beats.happened: By midday in London Brent crude was up about 1.4% to $93.71 a barrel and US crude up 1.5% to $86.97. The rise followed Iran's drone attack on a US radar in Bahrain and a ship hit twice in the Strait of Hormuz with its crew still missing. Traders also expect US crude stocks to fall, and US emergency reserves are at their lowest since 1982.
beats.means: The bounce is small next to the month's slide. Prices now sit in a range, with returning supply pulling down and repeated attacks pulling up.
beats.fx: Firmer oil gives slight support to the Canadian dollar and adds a little cost for importers such as Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: Fresh attacks on Gulf shipping and a US radar lift prices off recent lows.
Higher prices for Canada's main export give the currency a little support.

items.watch: Weekly US crude stock figures, and the OPEC+ meeting on November 29 on 2027 output.

items.headline: US homebuilder sentiment tumbles to more than 14-1/2-year low in November
items.story_title: How strong is the US economy?
items.summary: A monthly survey of US homebuilders fell to its weakest level since April 2012 in November, as high mortgage rates kept buyers away. Almost half of builders cut prices.

beats.was: The National Association of Home Builders asks builders each month how the market for new homes looks; a reading under 50 means more see it as poor. It stood at 29 in October, already weak, as mortgage rates climbed with Fed rate rises.
beats.happened: On Tuesday, November 17 the index dropped to 25, against forecasts for no change. Current sales, expected sales and buyer visits all fell. About 46% of builders cut prices and 68% gave buyers other deals, both the most since the pandemic.
beats.means: Housing is the part of the US economy hit first and hardest by higher borrowing costs, and it is now clearly struggling. It shows Fed rate rises are biting, even though shoppers kept spending in October.
beats.fx: A small weight on the dollar, but it did not shake the near-certain bets on a December Fed rise. Housing weakness matters more for the dollar if it starts to spread into jobs and spending.

impact.why: Housing slumping under high mortgage rates points to slower growth, though December Fed rise bets held.

items.watch: US housing starts and building permits for October: a sharp drop would show the slump spreading from mood into actual building.

items.headline: Banks call 4.85% rate peak despite Bullock's inflation warning
items.story_title: Has the Reserve Bank of Australia finished raising rates?
items.summary: Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Michele Bullock said the risks to inflation still lean upward and that the bank's rate rises were not only about oil. Major banks still think rates have peaked.

beats.was: The Reserve Bank of Australia has raised its cash rate five times this year, to 4.85%, the highest in 18 years. Minutes out the same day showed the last rise was a 6-3 vote, and many in the market think the bank is done.
beats.happened: Speaking at a regulator's forum on Tuesday, November 17, Bullock said inflation risks remain tilted higher. She added that the bank began raising rates before the Middle East war pushed up oil prices, so the rises were about more than fuel costs. Big lenders including ANZ and Commonwealth Bank, along with Goldman Sachs, still expect 4.85% to be the top.
beats.means: Bullock is pushing back on the idea that the bank is finished, but she did not signal another rise. The next decision is on December 8, and the gap between her tone and the banks' forecasts leaves the outcome open.
beats.fx: A little support for the Australian dollar from a governor who sounds ready to act again, but it is outweighed by a split board and the strong US dollar.

impact.why: The governor's firm tone helps, but banks still see the peak and the board is divided.

items.watch: Australian wage figures on Tuesday, November 17 evening US time and jobs figures on Thursday, November 19: strong numbers would back Bullock; weak ones would back the banks.

items.headline: New Zealand central bank warns global risks rising, says system can withstand them
items.story_title: Will the Reserve Bank of New Zealand raise rates on December 9?
items.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand said dangers to the world financial system keep growing, but New Zealand's banks are strong enough to cope. Strain on local households and firms has eased since last year.

beats.was: Twice a year the Reserve Bank of New Zealand reports on how safe the country's banks and borrowers are. Its policy rate is 2.75%, unemployment has risen to 5.7% and the bank decides on rates next on December 9.
beats.happened: In Tuesday's report the bank said global risks, including disruption to energy and trade from the Middle East conflict, are still building. It judged that New Zealand's financial system can absorb shocks, and said financial stress at home has come down from last year's peak, though unevenly across households and businesses.
beats.means: The report gives no reason to hold back on rates for financial-safety worries, so the December decision will turn on inflation and jobs. It adds little that is new for markets.
beats.fx: Close to neutral for the New Zealand dollar, which sat near 55 US cents and remains driven mostly by the strong US dollar.

impact.why: A sound banking system is reassuring, but warnings about rising global risk and a strong US dollar keep the kiwi low.

items.watch: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand's rate decision on December 9.

items.headline: RBA board judges fifth rate hike needed to provide policy assurance
items.story_title: Has the Reserve Bank of Australia finished raising rates?
items.summary: Minutes of the Reserve Bank of Australia's early-November meeting show a 6-3 split: most members raised rates to be safe on inflation, while three feared a sharper slowdown. They gave no hint about December.

beats.was: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised its cash rate on November 3 for the fifth time this year, to 4.85%, the highest in 18 years. Unemployment has climbed to a five-year high of 4.7% and house prices are falling.
beats.happened: The meeting record, out on Tuesday, November 17, shows six of nine members felt earlier rises might not be enough, because inflation has stayed above target for a long time and the economy still shows some strength. Three voted to hold, worried that rising joblessness and falling house prices could turn into a much sharper downturn.
beats.means: The board raised rates as insurance, not as the start of a new run, and a third of it already wants to stop. That fits market pricing that the peak has passed, with a small cut expected by the end of next year.
beats.fx: Little support for the Australian dollar: a split board and rate-cut pricing for 2027 leave it with less of a rate edge while US rates are expected to keep rising.

impact.why: A 6-3 split and no December hint back the view that Australian rates have peaked, while US rates are still climbing.

items.watch: Australian jobs figures and the fourth-quarter inflation reading: further rises in unemployment would strengthen the three members who wanted to stop.

items.headline: Canada's annual inflation rate holds at 3.1% in October
items.story_title: Will the Bank of Canada raise rates on December 9?
items.summary: Canadian inflation stayed at 3.1% in October, a touch below the 3.2% forecast. The Bank of Canada's preferred core measures sit close to its 2% goal, which weakens the case for a rate rise in December.

beats.was: Inflation in Canada was 3.1% in September, pushed up by fuel costs from the Middle East war. The Bank of Canada has said it is ready to raise rates if those energy costs spread into other prices, and it next decides on December 9.
beats.happened: Statistics Canada said prices rose 3.1% from a year earlier in October, against forecasts of 3.2%, and 0.2% from September. Without food and energy, inflation was 1.8%. The bank's own core measures came in at 2.0% for the median and 1.8% for the trimmed mean.
beats.means: Energy is lifting the headline number, but it is not spreading into everyday prices. That gives the Bank of Canada room to hold in December; bank ING sees January as the more likely time for any rise.
beats.fx: With fewer reasons for the Bank of Canada to act soon, the Canadian dollar has less support against a US dollar lifted by expected Fed rate rises. The US dollar was near 1.43 Canadian dollars, close to its October high.

impact.why: Slightly softer inflation and core near 2% make a December Bank of Canada rise less likely.
The gap between expected US and Canadian rate rises widens a little.

items.watch: Bank of Canada decision on December 9: a hold would confirm that energy costs are not yet a reason to raise rates.
